stories.topic: Lal Bihari Mritak: the man who had to prove he was alive
stories.summary: Lal Bihari was born in 1951 in Azamgarh, Uttar Pradesh. In 1976 his cousins wanted his land, so they paid bribes, produced a death certificate and had him declared officially dead. At 25 he set out to become alive again on paper. He staged his own funeral and claimed compensation for his 'widow'. He threw stones at a police station hoping to be arrested, since an arrest would prove he existed, but the bribed police simply ignored him. He kidnapped a 10-year-old cousin, expecting the family to come and settle things. Nobody came, so after ten days he bought the boy ice cream and sent him home. He contested elections against VP Singh in Allahabad in 1988 and against Rajiv Gandhi in Amethi in 1989, on the logic that a candidate on the rolls must be alive. He renamed himself Lal Bihari Mritak ('mritak' means dead) and founded the Uttar Pradesh Mritak Sangh, which grew to 20,000 members who had all been declared dead. He was finally declared alive in 1994. Of those 20,000 members, only four ever made it back.
stories.insight: This is the opening frame for the KYC problem. Once the state's paper version of you separates from the real you, the paper wins. Reversing a bureaucratic record is close to impossible: four out of twenty thousand. Amit also points out that behind every independent candidate who loses a deposit there may be a story like this one.
stories.quote: Imagine coming to terms with your own death, which has allegedly already happened and you're still alive.

stories.topic: Even a top banker couldn't get his KYC done
stories.summary: Harsh Vardhan is a very senior banking figure. He sits on boards, people respect his judgment, and he knows the people who run the banks. On The Seen and the Unseen he told Amit what a nightmare it had been to get his own KYC sorted out: endless phone calls to one place and then another.
stories.insight: If someone with direct access to bank leadership finds KYC painful, the system is not failing only at the edges. Privilege makes the pain smaller but does not remove it. Both hosts stress that it is far worse for people without such connections.
stories.quote: he told me about what a nightmare it was for him to get his KYC sorted out, that you make phone calls here, you make phone calls there.

stories.topic: A smart friend and an ageing father, defeated by paperwork
stories.summary: A very smart friend of Amit's, in her 40s, had a supplementary credit card linked to her husband's. She had completed KYC the year before. This year she could not get through the maze of paperwork in time and lost the card, while her husband kept his. Amit also remembers his father in his last years, fumbling and quite unable to cope with these demands.
stories.insight: KYC is an annual test of whether you can navigate a bureaucracy, and it hits the elderly hardest. Amit calls it plain cruelty to make people of advancing years prove themselves again and again.
stories.quote: And it was cruelty to expect a man of advancing years or a woman of advancing years to deal with all of this.

stories.topic: Al Capone's laundromats and the birth of 'money laundering'
stories.summary: In 1930s America, the gangster Al Capone ran criminal cash through cash-income businesses, namely laundromats, the shops where you load your clothes into a machine and collect them washed. The illicit money was shown as the laundromat's income, and that is where the term 'money laundering' comes from.
stories.insight: Every time the Enforcement Directorate is in the news, Ajay says, we are living with the consequences of states trying to block this gangster trick. A worldwide surveillance system grew out of it.
stories.quote: And so income would be shown as the money belonging to the laundromat, and that's how the word money laundering emerged.

stories.topic: 1933: Swiss bank secrecy as a defence against the Nazis
stories.summary: Banks had always kept their customers' affairs private as an informal norm. When Hitler came to power in 1933, Nazi Germany passed a law requiring every German citizen to disclose their overseas assets, something states had never done before. Switzerland was then the banking capital of the world, and it worried that informal codes would not protect its foreign customers. So it passed the first laws stating that no bank would divulge customer information except on the order of a Swiss judge prosecuting a crime under Swiss law. Foreign prosecutors were turned away.
stories.insight: Ajay turns the familiar populist story about Swiss banks and tax havens on its head. In the 20th century, people fled governments, and places like Switzerland were how ordinary people protected their wealth and private lives from authoritarian states. He also notes that the Nazi practice of demanding disclosure of overseas assets is now routine everywhere.
stories.quote: to understand the 20th century is to see that these are the ways by which people protected themselves against governments.

stories.topic: Russians amazed that the US Treasury taught them surveillance
stories.summary: A friend of Ajay's, an Indian official, had quiet private conversations with Russian counterparts. They told him, with real wonder, that the American Treasury was teaching them how to build a mass surveillance system in finance. They had not known how to build one themselves.
stories.insight: The post-9/11 anti-money-laundering push, led by the US, ended up handing authoritarian governments the know-how to watch their own citizens. Ajay calls this a blot on America's conscience.
stories.quote: did you know the American Treasury is teaching us how to oppress our own people?

stories.topic: Ajay's mea culpa on Aadhaar as the KYC fix
stories.summary: Ajay admits that he was among the finance people who thought Aadhaar would get around the KYC mess. Aadhaar arrived, the first number was issued in 2009, and in 2024 banks still demand fresh KYC every year while the AML-CFT burden continues.
stories.insight: It is unusual and useful to hear an expert say plainly that he was wrong, and the mistake carries a general lesson: you cannot accept bad institutions and paper over them with technology.
stories.quote: I am guilty. I'm part of this thought process. And in hindsight I realize how wrong it was.

recommendations.creator: FATF
recommendations.context: From Ajay's reading list in the show notes.
recommendations.reason: Shows the pressure behind FATF. Ajay explains that countries were offered a choice: join the financial surveillance regime or face more friction in the world.

core_ideas.explanation: A spy following you learns what you say, do and buy. A complete view of your finances reveals just as much. If surveillance of daily life is unacceptable in a liberal democracy, so is surveillance of financial life. The answer 'if you have nothing to hide' misses the point. Once you know you are watched you are in the panopticon, and you start bending your behaviour to suit the watcher. For Ajay, freedom is the world of not being observed. Amit adds a challenge: let anyone who uses that argument make their Google searches and incognito browsing public.
core_ideas.quote: So the simple proposition I want to put up is that if you believe in personal privacy, you should equally believe in financial privacy.

core_ideas.explanation: Modern populism grants individuals some privacy but treats companies as fair game for unlimited disclosure. Ajay disagrees. A firm's list of customers and vendors, handed to competitors or to powerful hostile people, can destroy the business, and financial statements alone reveal who a firm deals with. Treating a firm as having no privacy because it is 'some capitalist' is a mistake.
core_ideas.quote: It's like a death sentence to have the violation of the financial privacy of a firm.

core_ideas.concept: Financial privacy protects freedom of association
core_ideas.explanation: The right to form clubs, NGOs, parties and companies is basic to liberal democracy, and Ajay sees free speech and the rest as flowing from it. If the state can see who funds an organisation, powerful people can go after its funders. Detailed reporting requirements therefore undermine association itself. Amit's version: a ruling party can see who donates to the opposition and send the tax people after them.
core_ideas.quote: Then if you will shatter financial privacy, you have shattered right to association.

core_ideas.concept: Bring the wiretap model to finance
core_ideas.explanation: In liberal democracies privacy is the default. A police officer who wants a wiretap must convince a judge with prima facie evidence, the tap lasts only a fixed time, and it works only going forward because phone companies don't store past calls and SMS. There is no mass surveillance of everyone's phone. Ajay wants the same in finance. Customers should be able to tell their bank to delete transactions after three days, or even a millisecond. Police should need a warrant from something like a US FISA court to watch a proven suspect for a fixed period, say 90 days. Mass surveillance in finance should be shut down through constitutional law and the courts, building on the Puttaswamy ruling.
core_ideas.quote: It is only in a police state that a policeman's job is easy. We must make their life difficult.

core_ideas.concept: Walls made the interior life possible
core_ideas.explanation: Amit, drawing on Rahul Matthan, says privacy is a historical achievement. In hunter-gatherer bands everyone could see and hear everyone else. Early settlements had thin walls, and only later came thick walls, separate houses and separate bedrooms. Being alone and unobserved gave people a rich interior life, the space to think, try new things and challenge convention. Much of human progress depends on that solitude.
core_ideas.quote: And you're not alone if you know you're being watched.

core_ideas.concept: How financial surveillance crept in, one step at a time
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay traces the history. In 1933 Nazi Germany first required citizens to disclose overseas assets. In the 1970s the US IRS required banks to report transactions above $10,000, and nobody objected because it was 'only for tax evaders'. Nixon's war on drugs created the crime of money laundering, built on a 'predicate offence', and the FATF club grew up around it. Countries outside the club face extra friction, and India was the last country admitted. After 9/11 the US Treasury pushed AML-CFT on the whole world. The laws carry Orwellian names; Ajay says the US 'Banking Privacy Act' is really the destruction of privacy in banking.
core_ideas.quote: We have normalized oppression in the modern world.

core_ideas.concept: Following the money doesn't catch terrorists
core_ideas.explanation: After 9/11 the idea was that you could catch plots by tracing the $100,000 sent to Mohammed Atta. Ajay's counterexample is a 555 cigarette box packed with diamonds: it holds about $100,000 and passes X-ray machines. Monitor seven billion people and terrorists simply switch to other channels. He says it is now well known that this system has not disrupted terrorism. It has fouled up finance worldwide and given governments more information about their subjects.
core_ideas.quote: You want to move a hundred thousand dollars to Mohammed Atta, you just have to carry one cigarette case.

core_ideas.concept: Security theatre vs. the legibility grab
core_ideas.explanation: Amit describes the state's reflex after a crisis with Yes Minister's line: 'we must do something, this is something, let's do it'. He uses Bruce Schneier's term 'security theatre' for checks that only look like security, such as mall guards who check your car boot but never open the suitcase, or metal detectors that beep with no follow-up. A determined attacker will always find another way. He adds that the state often caused the problem in the first place, since Al Qaeda grew out of America arming guerrillas against the Russians in Afghanistan. Ajay separates the two cases. Airport checks are theatre, but financial surveillance is a public-choice grab: the state stokes fear of terrorists and takes legibility (James C. Scott's term) and power over citizens. Amit wants it the other way round: the state should be transparent to citizens, not citizens to the state.
core_ideas.quote: So they grab power over the people under the excuse of terrorism.

core_ideas.concept: Security vs. freedom is a false trade-off
core_ideas.explanation: The debate is usually framed as giving up some freedom to get security. Amit points out that surrendering freedom to the state also removes your security against the state, and nobody protects you from the state. So you lose both.
core_ideas.quote: So actually we lose both. When we lose our freedom, we lose our freedom and we lose our security.

core_ideas.concept: Why India's KYC is the world's worst: each layer covers itself
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay dislikes FATF rules, but in London, Zurich or Washington opening an account is fairly painless; it is like a stupid but tolerable airport check. In India the FATF rules get their harshest reading in the national rules. The RBI then makes them worse, the bank makes them worse again, and the frontline employee applies them in the worst possible way. No one at any step answers for the welfare of citizens. Poor people and small firms give up and fall back on cash, gold and real estate. The result is financial exclusion and a country where it gets harder to run a firm of five or forty people.
core_ideas.quote: My only objective is to cover my ass. So each one comes up with a harder and crazier version of it.

core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's general law: technology cannot fix a malfunctioning state. Aadhaar was meant to end the KYC nightmare, but banks still demand fresh KYC every year. Amit argues for not letting the perfect be the enemy of the good: why not a simple central order that Aadhaar is enough? Ajay replies with public choice. Officials who want to protect themselves will keep adding rules, so hoping good sense will prevail is the mistake. The real work is fixing institutions, which he calls the hard work of the humanities and liberal arts.
core_ideas.quote: Adding CPUs to a malfunctioning Indian government never makes the Indian government better. CPUs are never the answer.

core_ideas.explanation: Drawing on Lant Pritchett and on Kelkar and Shah, Ajay argues that policies which seem to work in the US depend on invisible supports there: liberal democracy, checks and balances, courts, communities and norms. Copy the policy without those supports and it does far worse. He calls it wrong, dangerous and evil of the US Treasury to push financial surveillance on the world, and stupid of India to accept it.
core_ideas.quote: be skeptical about global best practice, that any naive transplantation of something that seems to work well in the United States should never be brought into India because there is so much other invisible infrastructure.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: The cold open is a KYC check on the co-host. Amit: "I'm not sure if this is my good friend Ajay. Bearded economists look alike to me. Are you Ajay Shah? Prove to me that you're Ajay Shah. Kaagaz dikhaao!" Ajay: "I don't have papers. Will you recognize my face? FRT, face recognition technology." Amit: "Biometrics. Take off your glasses, I'll scan your eyes." Amit then introduces himself as "Amit allegedly".
Amit on the police facing Lal Bihari's stones: "the police, for the first time in recorded Indian history, take a Gandhian view of the situation and ignore the stones."
On Lal Bihari's failed kidnapping: "India's population is awesome. There are many kids in that family, no one gives a shit." After ten days he gives the boy ice cream and sends him home.

A running gag casts the episode's cameraman Vaishnav Vyas as Lal Bihari in the film version. Amit says behind every independent candidate who loses a deposit there is a story "rich in life, rich in drama, rich in pathos. Rich in cinematic potential. Are you listening, Vaishnav Vyas?"
Ajay on why his bank wants yearly re-KYC: "Like proofs have the depreciation and they vanish with time, so it has to be re-upped."
Amit on the 'nothing to hide' argument: he dares its defenders to make their Google search results public. "What do you do in the Chrome incognito window? Everybody has a private life, boss."
Amit on a reported plot to hide bombs in breast implants: "You're not gonna say take out your breast implants and put them on the security tray."

Ajay sings The Police: "Every vow you break, every claim you stake, I'll be watching you. This has been traditionally thought of as a creepy male stalker song, but gentle readers, please email this to all the civil servants in your life." Amit: "The state is a creepy male stalker. And much worse."
Amit, after saying The Lives of Others shows how watching can change both watcher and watched: "So I don't think the Indian state is really going to get reformed because they're watching us."

Post-credits, Amit explains why he wants privacy: it isn't shame about "all the unspeakable things we do. It is a question of what will happen to you when you see what we are doing... It will destroy your lives. You will dream at night of the fun that I have. So don't surveil me..."
Yes Minister's political logic, quoted by Amit as the state's reflex after a terror attack: "we must do something, this is something, let's do it."
Bruce Schneier's term "security theater": security that is performed rather than real.
James C. Scott's "state legibility", used by Amit for what financial surveillance gives the state: a view into people's lives.
Ajay quotes "the great man" on liberty and safety, with the terms swapped: "those who will sacrifice security in exchange for freedom will end up with neither security nor freedom."
"That old saw of power corrupts, absolute power corrupts absolutely", invoked by Amit to explain what a state does with surveillance power: crack down on dissent and political opponents.
The Puttaswamy ruling, which Ajay says must be the constitutional basis for financial privacy alongside personal privacy.
Israel's exploding pagers, cited by Amit as proof that a clever enough adversary always finds a way around security.
Lal Bihari's electoral campaigns against VP Singh in Allahabad (1988) and Rajiv Gandhi in Amethi (1989), contested just to prove he was alive.
